name: Winter production
summary: Growing berries to fruit outside a region's normal season -- through protected culture, counter-season geography, or low-chill varieties -- to reach markets when local supply is otherwise absent.
what_is_it: Winter production refers to growing berries so they fruit outside the region's traditional season, most commonly through protected culture (high tunnels, greenhouses, substrate systems), counter-season geography (Southern Hemisphere production supplying Northern Hemisphere winter demand, or vice versa), or varieties with low chill requirements suited to warmer regions.
why_it_matters: Winter or counter-season production captures premium pricing when local/seasonal supply is absent, and is a major driver of both international trade flows in berries and continued investment in protected-culture growing systems and low-chill variety breeding.
how_evaluated: Winter-production capability is assessed at the system/region level -- whether a production system, growing region, or variety's chill requirement actually supports fruiting in the target off-season window -- rather than through a single measurable trait on the fruit itself.
what_affects_it: Chill-hour requirement of the variety, availability and cost of protected-culture infrastructure, regional climate, and market access/logistics for reaching demand during the target window all determine whether winter production is viable.
how_to_interpret: Winter-production claims are regional and system-dependent -- a variety or growing approach that supports winter production in one climate zone will not automatically do so elsewhere. Treat winter-production claims the same way as other regional production-practice claims: look for the specific geography and growing system before generalizing.
